articles.title: Maha audit flags irregularities in ₹37.61-crore malaria spending; Abitkar vows action
articles.description: The audit report points to lapses in tendering, including failure to constitute purchase committees, publish newspaper advertisements and use the Centre’s Government e-Marketplace portal. It also alleges that preferred suppliers were awarded contracts.

articles.title: POWERGRID: What strong oversight looks like
articles.description: Every Kashmiri who has watched a 400 kV tower rise on a hillside, through an orchard or across a village path has seen how large these projects are. Many have also wondered how a project of this scale is governed. Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) is a Maharatna public sector company and the backbone of the national transmission network. It carries our hydropower out in summer and brings in power when winter demand outstrips local generation. It also shapes where lines run, which trees are felled and how landowners are compensated. I write as an environmental scientist, a former regulator and a certified Independent Director. This author appreciates the work of POWERGRID’s engineers and linemen, who operate in some of the hardest terrain in the country. But at the same a, governance question comes to mind. What should independent oversight of a company like this look like? How closely does the public record show it, especially for Jammu & Kashmir? A strong company The starting point is a company that performs. According to PSU Connect’s report on its FY26 results, POWERGRID earned standalone net profit of ₹15,921 crore for 2025-26 and is paying a total dividend of ₹9 per share. Its own Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 records record capital expenditure of ₹39,967 crore, and PSU Watch’s report on the 37th annual general meeting says the company operates 292 substations and about 1.87 lakh circuit km of lines, with availability above 99.8%. The company’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) for 2025-26 says its core indicators carry reasonable assurance from TÜV India, a higher standard than many listed companies meet. The same report says Scope 1 and 2 emissions fell 17.95% in 2025-26 and that renewable reached 35.74% of its energy mix. These achievements are the base for any fair discussion. What the public registry shows, and what it cannot Most citizens would look first at the corporate registry. ZaubaCorp’s profile, compiled from Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) filings records POWERGRID’s Corporate Identification Number as L40101DL1989GOI038121, incorporation on 23 October 1989 as National Power Transmission Corporation Ltd, registration with the Registrar of Companies, Delhi, and classification as a Union government company. Authorised capital is ₹10,000 crore and paid-up capital ₹9,300.6 crore. It names directors including Ravisankar Ganesan, Ravindra Kumar Tyagi, Yatindra Dwivedi, Abhay Choudhary, Chetan Bansilal Kankariya, Saibaba Darbamulla, Lalit Bohra and Ram Naresh. The same page shows the limits of such aggregators. It lists the last annual general meeting as 30 August 2023 and the last balance sheet as 31 March 2023, although the notice of the 37th AGM confirms the company met on 20 August 2026. Assets, revenue and profit are blank, the member count reads zero and the complaints tables are empty. This is a lag in a third-party database, not evidence of any violation. It does mean that a citizen in Srinagar or Kishtwar who relies on it will learn little about how the board handles environmental and community risk. For that, the exchange filings, annual report and sustainability report are the better record. Independent oversight: why continuity matters The corporate governance filing that POWERGRID lodged with NSE for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 shows a board of ten with three independent directors, and records compliance with Regulation 17 of the SEBI Listing Regulations as “No”. The three, Rohit Vaswani, Shiv Tapasya Paswan and Smt. Sajal Jha, were appointed on 16 April and 16 May 2025. The company’s Annual Secretarial Compliance Report for 2025-26 explains that the board had no independent directors from November 2024, when two tenures ended, and that quorum could not always be met. The company’s stated position in both documents is that the President of India appoints independent directors through the Ministry of Power, and that it has repeatedly taken up the vacancies with the Ministry. The secretarial report adds that NSE and BSE each fined the company ₹14,39,600 for the March 2025 quarter and later waived the fines, on 12 September and 7 October 2025. The three directors have since completed their tenures. Scanx reported that Paswan and Vaswani finished on 15 April 2026, and a second Scanx headline says Jha’s tenure ended on 15 May 2026; each served about a year. I found no announcement of replacements. PSU Watch’s account of the 37th AGM on 20 August 2026 names only executives and a government nominee among the directors present. Market Screener’s board listing shows no independent director. I could not open the filing for the June 2026 quarter, so readers should check the company’s latest NSE and BSE announcements. If the position stands, it is a gap that belongs to the appointment process as much as to the company. The lesson is not about blame. The audit, nomination, stakeholder and risk committees all depend on independent members to function as designed, and short tenures and gaps make it hard to build the institutional memory that good oversight needs. The secretarial compliance report also notes that board-evaluation requirements were treated as not applicable under a 2017 MCA exemption for government companies. SEBI granted relief from Regulations 17(10) and 25(4) by a letter dated 2 March 2026. These are lawful accommodations. They do mean that the usual checks on directors apply more lightly to government companies, which makes the voluntary quality of governance more important. Who owns sustainability? In the documents I could read, there is no board committee or independent director with an ESG or sustainability mandate. The FY2025-26 BRSR names Naveen Srivastava, Director (Operations), as the highest authority for the business responsibility policy and the decision-maker on sustainability issues, with Vibhay Kumar, Executive Director (ESG & Net Zero), as the contact. The NSE governance filing lists the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, Stakeholders Relationship and Risk Management committees, with an executive director chairing risk. The annual report describes a four-tier ESG structure, although the extract I read did not give its detail. Executive ownership of sustainability is sensible. Adding an independent chair for a sustainability committee would give the board a second line of oversight, which is good practice for a company with POWERGRID’s footprint. What the law provides, and where it stops The Companies Act 2013 is stronger than many assume. Section 166(2) asks every director to act in good faith for the company, its employees, shareholders and community, and for the protection of the environment. Section 149 and Schedule IV define the independent director’s role and Section 135 governs corporate social responsibility. These are duties of conduct, enforced by shareholders and regulators. A landowner cannot invoke them directly. The structure of the group adds another layer. Much newer transmission is built in single-project special purpose companies. Under Rule 4 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, as amended in 2017, unlisted wholly owned subsidiaries, joint ventures and dormant companies need not appoint independent directors. Regulation 24 of the SEBI Listing Regulations requires a listed parent to place at least one of its independent directors on an unlisted material subsidiary. This is a reasonable policy choice, but it means the company that builds and operates a line may have no independent director of its own. On disclosure, Regulation 34(2)(f) requires a BRSR, with assured core indicators for the top 1,000 listed companies. POWERGRID meets this. The BRSR is, however, a company-wide document. In the portions I could read, for both 2024-25 and 2025-26, it gives no state-wise breakdown and no mention of Jammu & Kashmir. On the ground in Kashmir These design choices matter because of what happens on land of the natives. On 10 September 2026 Justice Rajnesh Oswal of the J&K and Ladakh High Court dismissed Ghulam Ahmad Malla v. State of J&K, a petition by landowners at Dreygam, Budgam, whose walnut trees were damaged when a 220 kV line was laid across their land. As the judgment records, the Horticulture Department had assessed their losses at ₹6,92,810, ₹5,13,130 and ₹12,10,380 under government orders of 1985 and 1995 (SRO 493 and SRO 386). The owners accepted payment without protest and took the felled wood. The court held that, having accepted it, they could not argue it was below market rates, and noted they had not challenged the SROs themselves. Their claim over the land under the line was not separately decided. The company followed the prescribed schedule. The lesson is that the schedule itself, now decades old, is where reform is needed. On trees at scale, The Wire reported in December 2018, in its headline, that the J&K government had approved cutting about 60,000 trees in 2015 for power lines. I could read only the headline and description, so I cite it as a pointer. The question it raises is still fair. Where is the public tally of trees felled for transmission in J&K, and where are the compensatory plantations? The BRSR describes forest avoidance and compensatory afforestation in general terms and gives no J&K figures. Then the valleys. T&D India reported in January 2025 that Ratle (850 MW) and Kiru (624 MW) on the Chenab in Kishtwar are joint ventures of NHPC and the J&K Power Development Corporation. Their evacuation scheme, Part A, was estimated at ₹1,214 crore, and Part B, a ₹196 crore reconductoring of the Kishenpur-Kishtwar line, goes to the Part A winner. According to IndiGrid, the Part A company, Ratle Kiru Power Transmission Ltd, owns 359 circuit km of 400 kV double-circuit line, 4 km to Kishtwar, 67 km to Kishenpur and 288 km to Jalandhar. IndiGrid, a private infrastructure trust, acquired it from REC Power Development and Consultancy on 24 March 2025, and the lines are under construction on a 35-year service agreement. The ownership chain runs from a public tender to a private trust, which is why a clear grievance address for local people matters. This is also a district that has seen cloudburst and landslide disasters, so slope and climate-risk studies deserve a visible place in project governance. What Kashmir receives, and what it cannot yet see The BRSR reports CSR spending of ₹391.16 crore in 2025-26 across more than 120 projects, while the annual report gives ₹382 crore, and the two figures should be reconciled. The BRSR also says a grievance mechanism exists, and that community complaints were 366 in 2025-26, with 28 pending at year end, against 349 and none pending in the previous year’s report. A pending count that has gone from zero to 28 is worth watching and worth explaining publicly. What the reports do not show is Jammu & Kashmir specifically. The only mention of the region’s neighbourhood in the annual report extract I read is a photograph caption of the Drass substation in Ladakh. A citizen cannot tell whether our share of CSR, jobs and compensation is proportionate to the assets we host. CSR also differs from compensation. Section 135 spending is a statutory obligation on profit, not payment for land crossed or trees felled. Finally, hosting national infrastructure raises a wider question about the fair share of benefits from J&K’s rivers and land, which belongs in public debate. None of this is a failing unique to POWERGRID. It is a gap in how national companies report on the regions where they work. Six practical proposals Good governance improves through specific, answerable steps. Several of this rest with the company, others with the Ministry of Power, SEBI and the J&K government. Continuity of independent oversight. Appoint independent directors for terms long enough to build experience and avoid gaps between tenures. A sustainability committee with an independent chair. Give community and climate risk a named board-level owner. State-wise disclosure. Publish CSR spend, land acquired, trees felled, compensatory plantations and grievances for Jammu & Kashmir in the BRSR or annual report. Independent voices on project companies. Extend the Regulation 24 principle so that companies building lines in sensitive terrain have at least one independent director. Current compensation rates. Update the 1985 and 1995 schedules to market-based rates for trees and for land under towers and lines with a right to contest. Slope-risk studies and a local grievance address. Publish geotechnical and cloudburst-risk studies before lines go up in districts like Kishtwar and name a J&K nodal officer with a public complaints register. POWERGRID has the scale, the finances and the track record to lead on all six. Independent oversight that is visible where the company works would strengthen the company, its shareholders and the people who live beside its lines. Note on evidence: The annual report and BRSR were read in extracts, the governance chapter of the annual report was not available to me, and the filing for the June 2026 quarter could not be opened. articles.title: Contractors meet Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar, seek release of Rs 38,000 cr in dues
articles.description: Alleging that tenders are being called for unfunded works, the association has demanded an immediate stop to this practice.
